signal.title: Act on the signal, not on the form.
signal.text: A CRM starts existing once someone has already raised their hand. BEE starts earlier: a funding round, a key hire, a stack change. By the time the lead reaches your CRM, the conversation should already be open.

hive.title: The whole market in one view.
hive.text: Not a list sorted by when it was imported — the entire market with every account's intent at once. Hot sits at the centre, lukewarm at the edges: you see where to look before reading a single name.

window.title: The moment, not just the contact.
window.text: Every account has weeks when it decides and months when it doesn't. BEE estimates that window and sorts by real urgency, not by age in the pipeline.

pipeline.title: The board you already know, fed by something no CRM has.
pipeline.text: Five stages, drag between columns, closes in green: from the outside it's a board. The difference is where the cards come from — nobody types them in, they arrive from the signal, already scored and with their play written.

play.title: A play that's ready, not a list of chores.
play.text: Argument, channel and timing, written for that account and that trigger. An intent tool tells you who; BEE also tells you what to say, and its AI is our own — not a generic chat bolted on the side.

sales.title: The result, closed and measured.
sales.text: Won per month against your target, with the team ranking and the real win rate. It's the only part of BEE painted green, because it's the only part talking about money collected.

learn.title: Every close corrects the next play.
learn.text: Won and lost feed back in: which argument worked, on which channel, at which moment. A CRM stores the outcome; BEE uses it. That's the loop no list tool can close.

network.title: The shortest path already exists.
network.text: Before writing cold, BEE checks whether someone on your team already has a route into that account. A warm intro beats the best cold sequence, and that route was already sitting in your own data.

soluciones.heroTitle: The same capabilities, shaped by the problem you have.
soluciones.heroSubtitle: There isn't a different version of BEE per segment — there's one system that solves a different problem depending on the size and shape of your sales team.

sdr.pain: Manual prospecting that eats hours before the first call.
sdr.fit: The signal engine prioritizes which account to go after first, and the daily brief builds the context — less time researching, more time talking to warm prospects.

founders.pain: No one dedicated to watching the market or deciding who to prioritize.
founders.fit: BEE does that background work — it detects the signal, enriches it, and suggests the next action, without needing to hire an analyst for it.

agencies.pain: Managing the pipeline for several accounts at once, each at its own pace.
agencies.fit: The revenue simulator projects the impact of ramping up prospecting per segment, account by account, before committing the team's hours.

scaleup.pain: Lead volume has already outgrown what a human can prioritize by hand.
scaleup.fit: Multi-channel automation designs sequences that advance on their own based on how each lead responds — always with human approval before anything sends.

quienesSomos.heroTitle: A sales team shouldn't waste time hunting for the signal.

finalDecision.title: The final call is always yours
finalDecision.description: BEE prepares the play — the message, the channel, the moment — but no external action goes out without your explicit approval.

weBuildWhatWeDescribe.title: We build what we describe

meta.title: Security — BEE
meta.description: How BEE isolates your data, authenticates every call, and logs every decision.

seguridad.heroTitle: Built so connecting your CRM isn't a risk.
seguridad.heroSubtitle: These aren't sales-page promises — they're mechanisms that exist today in BEE's backend, the same ones behind the guarantees on the rest of the site.

multiTenant.title: Real multi-tenant isolation
multiTenant.body: Every table that stores account data is scoped by organization — not an optional flag someone can forget to turn on, but part of the data model from the design stage. An endpoint that doesn't filter by your organization simply cannot return data from another account.

layeredAuth.title: Layered authentication
layeredAuth.body: User sessions use a signed JWT with a 7-day expiration. Service-to-service access (integrations, the frontend itself) uses a separate API key — two distinct trust boundaries, not one shared secret for everything.

hmacWebhooks.title: HMAC-signed webhooks
hmacWebhooks.body: Every incoming webhook is validated against an HMAC signature before processing. Signature verification is on by default in production — turning it off is an explicit decision, not the default behavior.

secrets.title: Secrets that never touch the code or the database
secrets.body: Credentials for external providers are read only from environment variables. They're never persisted in the database or written to a log — when something needs to show up in a diagnostic message, the real value is masked.

auditTrail.title: Every agent decision is logged
auditTrail.body: The system keeps an audit trail of automated decisions — which signal triggered which action, and when. It isn't a black box: there's a chain of decisions that can be reconstructed.

humanApproval.title: No external send without human approval
humanApproval.body: The engine prepares the next action — the message, the channel, the moment — but an email, a LinkedIn message, or a full sequence never goes out without a person giving explicit go-ahead.

meta.title: Documentation — how BEE works inside
meta.description: BEE's architecture, its languages, the path a signal takes, and what's still missing. Written for whoever is about to read or extend the code.

documentacion.heroSubtitle: Not API docs — the architecture, the languages and the decisions, for whoever picks up the code and wants to understand it before touching it. At the end, the roadmap: what BEE can do and what it still lacks.

blocks.text: BEE is a monorepo with two applications that share no code and deploy separately. They speak only over HTTP, through a versioned API. That boundary is deliberate: the brain has to survive a complete rewrite of the frontend.

apps/
├── api/    FastAPI · SQLModel · PostgreSQL · Alembic
└── web/    Next.js (App Router) · TypeScript · Tailwind · shadcn/ui

In production they are two separate projects on the same host. The frontend knows the backend through a single variable (NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL) and nothing else; the backend doesn't know the frontend exists, beyond the list of origins it accepts in CORS.
Never merge them into one deployment. That independence is what lets the frontend be replaced without touching the engine, and lets each scale when it — not the other — asks for it.
Nothing exotic and nothing for fashion: every choice solves a concrete problem and can be swapped without dragging the rest with it.

rows: The ecosystem where the data and model work BEE will need already lives.
Real types in the signatures; validation and the OpenAPI schema generated from the same code.
Joins SQLAlchemy and Pydantic: one definition is both the table and the API contract.
Relational, with extensions — pgvector is already enabled for embeddings.
Every schema change is a versioned, reversible revision, never a create_all().
Domain types are mirrored by hand from the backend schemas.
Server components by default; the client only where there is interaction.
Every colour comes from BEE tokens; no loose values.
Cache, retries and revalidation without writing a single reducer.
Spanish and English, with no route segment and no locale middleware.
Off by default. See the background jobs section.

blocks.text: The backend is strictly layered and the dependency always points inward. A layer may call the one below, never the one above.

api/           HTTP routes: validate, authenticate, delegate. No business logic.
  ↓
services/      the brain: scoring, strategies, permissions, integrations.
  ↓
repositories/  data access: queries, per-organization filtering.
  ↓
models/        the SQLModel tables and their invariants.

The practical rule: if a function in api/ has an if that decides something about the business, it is in the wrong layer. And if a service writes a select() by hand instead of asking a repository, it skipped the layer that guarantees the organization filter.
This is the product's central route. Everything else hangs off it.

items: A signed webhook arrives at POST /api/v1/signals/webhook. The sender's HMAC signature is verified and the tenant resolved — nothing enters without an organization.
The engine runs the signal past every applicable analyzer and aggregates their verdicts into a score.
The signal is persisted, and if the score qualifies an opportunity is born with its buying window and its strategy: argument, channel, timing. Answers 201.

External providers come in through a different door, POST /api/v1/webhooks/receive: that one answers 202 Accepted in milliseconds and queues the enrichment, so the sender never waits on a third-party call.
The queued work is drained by a cron every minute (see the background jobs section).
The outcome of the close — won or lost — feeds back and adjusts the next play.

blocks.text: The two doors differ on purpose: /signals/webhook does the work and answers 201 with the result; /webhooks/receive promises and queues. That 202 means "accepted", not "processed" — what makes it real is the durable queue in the next section.
Signal types change constantly, so the engine doesn't know them — it discovers them. An analyzer is a class with a decorator, and adding one requires touching no other part of the system.

Eleven are registered today: funding, hiring, tech adoption, franchise expansion, mergers and acquisitions, public tenders, regulatory change, grants, behaviour, a generic fallback and an LLM-based one.
The LLM analyzer is optional. With AI_PROVIDER=none — the default — BEE runs entirely on rules: zero cost, zero external latency and no dependency on any provider.
Every table holding customer data carries organization_id, and all 39 that do have an index led by that column, created in the same migration that creates the table.
Isolation is not trusted to each query: it lives in shared helpers (scope_to_organization, scope_by_organization_id, get_visible_user_ids). A query that skips them is a security bug, not a shortcut.
Hard rule in this repository: no new endpoint or query over an organization's data is written without going through those helpers.
BEE uses no Supabase and no identity provider. The session is a JWT the backend signs itself.

items: The token carries the minimum: user id, organization id, role and expiry.
On every request, get_current_user reloads the user from the database and re-checks role and is_active. Deactivating someone cuts their access immediately, even with a still-valid token.
Registration creates the organization and its first OWNER user in a single transaction; the email is globally unique.
There is a second, independent secret (API_SECRET_KEY) for service-to-service calls, and a third (SUPPORT_ADMIN_SECRET) for two internal tools. Leaking one does not compromise the others.

blocks.text: Starlette inserts each middleware at the front of the stack, so the last one registered is the outermost. In BEE that order is chosen, not inherited:

CORS                  ← outermost: answers the preflight OPTIONS
  └ UnhandledError    ← turns an exception into a JSON 500
     └ RateLimit      ← per IP, before asking for the key
        └ APIKey      ← requires X-API-Key except on public routes
           └ Security ← headers on every response, errors included

CORS goes outside because a browser never attaches custom headers to a preflight: if the API key were evaluated first, every preflight would die with a 401 and the browser would never send the real request. And the per-IP limit sits before the key so a client hammering with invalid keys is throttled too, instead of getting 401s for free forever.
This is the part that needs the most care on a serverless deployment, and the one that most easily breaks in silence.

Without Redis, queueing means an asyncio.Queue inside the process. On a long-lived server that is fine; inside a serverless function, when the instance freezes the queued work disappears — and the webhook already answered 202.

With Redis the queue is durable and a cron drains it every minute. A job that fails is rescheduled with exponential backoff until its retries run out, and then moves to a dead-letter queue that can be inspected and replayed.

rows: Shared state for the abuse limits, which are per-instance without it.
The durable queue instead of the in-process one.
The scheduled ticks. Without it those routes answer 404 on purpose.

blocks.text: A warning learned the hard way: turn Redis on for queues and limits, but leave the notification stream off on serverless. Every open tab holds a function for 60 seconds in a loop, and that is billed by the second.

44 tables and 52 Alembic revisions. create_all() never runs in production: startup compares the database's revision against the one the code expects and shouts in the log if they differ, and /api/v1/ready answers 503 while there is drift.
Migrations apply themselves on every push that touches migrations or models. If the database secret is missing, the step fails — it does not warn and carry on.

That last sentence is a scar. The step used to exit successfully when the secret was missing, showed a green check, and the database fell 26 revisions behind until a login started failing. A step that might do nothing must fail.

items: App Router with server components by default. "use client" only where there is state or events, and the further down the tree, the better.
Domain types live in src/types/domain.ts, mirrored by hand from the backend schemas. When one side changes, the other changes.
The public sandbox (/probar) does not call the API: it reads and writes a demo store in the browser, seeded from sample data. That is why it works with no account and no backend.
The design system rules: all colour comes from BEE tokens, one hue per box at three intensities, green only where closed money is the subject, and no coloured text or icons.
The charts are our own and measure their box: no box is left with white space, and none deforms with long data.

pruebas.title: Tests and how to run it

blocks.text: The backend suite is 1,277 tests and it is hermetic: it runs on in-memory SQLite, with no Postgres, no Redis and no network. The whole thing runs in a couple of minutes, and it is where most of this project's regressions have been caught.

# Backend
cd apps/api
uv venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
pytest                      # 1,277 tests, no external services
ruff check app tests
uvicorn app.main:app --reload

# Frontend
cd apps/web
pnpm install
pnpm dev                    # http://localhost:3000

# Everything at once: Postgres + Redis + migrations + API + cron
docker compose up --build

documentacion.roadmapIntro: What BEE can do today, and what it lacks. Written so whoever takes the code knows where the edge is before starting.
roadmapNow: Signal ingestion by webhook with HMAC signature, isolated per organization.
Eleven pluggable analyzers; adding one touches nothing else.
Scored opportunities with a buying window and a written strategy (argument, channel, timing).
A five-stage CRM board with drag between columns and closes in green.
Sales, Forecast, Calendar, Network, Sequences, Brand voice and Control.
Real multi-tenancy with teams, roles and hierarchy-based visibility.
A public sandbox with no signup, running on sample data in the browser.
Spanish and English across the whole product.
Versioned, automatic migrations with schema-drift detection.

roadmapNext.title: Email verification
roadmapNext.text: Registration hands out a session without verifying the address, and emails are globally unique: someone can claim another company's address and lock its real owner out. This is the blocker for opening signup.

roadmapNext.title: Outbound email (SMTP)
roadmapNext.text: With no provider configured, password recovery writes to the log and delivers nothing. It also blocks the verification above: they are one problem, not two.

roadmapNext.title: Redis
roadmapNext.text: Turns on the durable queue — today a queued job is lost when the function freezes — and makes the abuse limits global instead of per-instance.

roadmapNext.title: File storage
roadmapNext.text: An avatar is stored as a data URI inside the user's row, up to 300 KB, in the table reloaded on every authenticated request. It belongs in a blob store, with only the URL kept.

roadmapNext.title: Rep progress on the server
roadmapNext.text: Milestones live in localStorage with no user id: switching computers resets the progress and two people sharing a browser share it. For a product built on gamification, that has to be a server fact.

roadmapNext.title: httpOnly cookie session with refresh
roadmapNext.text: Today it is a single token in localStorage, with no rotation and no revocation. It works, but any XSS takes the whole session.

roadmapNext.title: Live notifications off serverless
roadmapNext.text: The stream exists and degrades cleanly to polling, but holding long connections inside functions is billed by the second. It needs its own runtime before being switched on.

roadmapNext.title: Organization dedupe by domain
roadmapNext.text: The second employee from the same company creates a parallel organization with nothing stopping them. Detecting the domain and offering 'request access' fixes it.

roadmapNext.title: Per-team currency with historical rates
roadmapNext.text: Currency is already stored per team; what's missing is converting amounts that arrive in signals using the rate on the day of the event, never today's, so history doesn't move.

roadmapNext.title: Composite indexes
roadmapNext.text: The organization filter is already indexed on all 39 tables. What comes next — organization plus status plus date — is decided with EXPLAIN ANALYZE over real data, not by inspection.
